Personally I recommend Debian. Many people will recommend Ubuntu & Linux Mint, but both of those are based on the unstable branch of Debian, and I feel include a lot of bloat and many unnecessary bugs. I've had a good experience with Debian stable (ver. 8 / Jessie). Good luck!

So I'll admit, I have been leaning towards Mint - Cinnamon so far. The reason being that I plan on changing my Wife's computer over as well, and I want something easy for her to use. Also, it seems (from a few USB boot trials) that Mint just works out-of-the-box with all her laptop's hardware (she has a Lenovo u410), and I've read it can be difficult to get laptops running smoothly with certain distros.

Are there any particular reasons you recommend Debian over Mint? I can't tell the difference between different distros except as far as the GUI is concerned, really. Mint just seems to have everything where I expect it to be.

If that is your experience with Mint, then use that. As you develop your skills using Linux you may like to give Debian a try, but for now settle on what works.

  • Mint has inherited many Ubuntu bugs for me in the past. My experience with Debian was that it was the smoothest experience & least amount of hiccups I had had setting up an install.

  • There is also the fact that Debian is the backbone of Ubuntu & Mint, and I feel more confident going with something which is such a mainstay & stable.

  • Depending on what flavor of Mint you use, it is based on Ubuntu. Ubuntu has had some controversy surrounding it in the community for piping ads through its desktop search via a partnership with Amazon. Richard Stallman has been very critical of this move, calling it spyware by definition. Mint should have all of this stripped out, but there is the issue of trust and diligence on the part of the Mint developers.

  • Debian is completely volunteer based, and adheres to a strict moral code in the direction the team takes. Ubuntu is backed by Canonical, which is a company which attempts to sustain itself with many business models. Mint makes revenue from advertisers on their website and from ads in their search pages when you open a browser, but mostly from donations.
I use it all the time, I just need to learn how to use it like a Linux expert.
